stories.title: 'I chase eclipses around the world'
stories.summary: A film-maker talks about eclipse-hunting worldwide after covering his first one in Alderney in 1999.
stories.post: 📰 NEWS: 'I chase eclipses around the world'. A film-maker talks about eclipse-hunting worldwide after covering his first one in Alderney in 1999. Source: BBC Science.
article_sentences: The spectacle of the total eclipse in 1999 in the Channel Islands was a "life-changing moment" for Dr Chris Riley who has become a "part-time eclipse chaser" ever since, travelling all over the world to see them.
The scientist was part of the team broadcasting Eclipse Live for the BBC in 1999.
He had been due to view the eclipse from Cornwall but was sent to Alderney the day before and said "it was the most amazing experience of my life".

He was there at the last spot in the British Isles to enjoy the spectacle, with broadcaster Jamie Theakston, in a show which attracted 13 million viewers and said watching the darkness rush in "really sends the hairs on the back of your neck up, it's a pretty special thing".
He told BBC Guernsey: "The first time you do anything is always perhaps the most special and, with an eclipse, it is particularly the case.
"You could really see the colour of the water change as this huge wall of darkness rushed towards us at 2,000 miles an hour."
They were joined by 250 astronomers for the total eclipse for a bird's eye view at the top of the island.
At the time scientist and film-maker Riley said: "We've just stood in the shadow of the moon."
There was this eerie twilight around us 360 degrees.
He added: "You could literally see the sky darkening behind us and this huge wall of darkness rushing over our heads and out towards France."
